fields.h1: The Cost of Following Jesus: Counting It, and Why It's Worth It
fields.meta_title: The Cost of Following Jesus — Counting It, and Why It's Worth It
fields.description: Jesus told people to count the cost before following him. Here is what following him actually costs, why he was so honest about it, and why it is still worth everything.
fields.body_html:
Most invitations play down the cost. Jesus did the opposite. To crowds eager to follow him, he said things designed to thin the ranks: take up a cross, sit down and count the cost, be ready to lose your life. He was not trying to be off-putting. He was being honest — more honest than much of the preaching that has come since. Following Jesus costs everything. And, as generations of his followers have found, it is still the best bargain a human being can make.

Here is what following Jesus actually costs, why he insisted on naming it up front, and why those who paid it have never regretted it.

Jesus told us to count the cost

“Which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?” (Luke 14:28). Jesus wanted no one signing up under false advertising. In the same breath he named the terms: “whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:27). The cross, to his hearers, was not jewelry; it was an instrument of death. To follow Jesus is to bring your own self-rule to that cross.

It is worth pausing on how out of step this is with how we usually recruit people to anything. We minimize the cost; Jesus maximized it. We promise ease; he promised a cross. On one occasion, when the crowds were largest and most eager, he turned and told them the terms so plainly that many walked away. He was not indifferent to whether people followed — he wept over those who would not — but he refused to win them on false pretenses. He wanted disciples who knew what they were signing, because only those who have counted the cost will still be standing when it comes due. That honesty is itself a mark of how much he valued them: he would rather have a few who understood than a crowd who did not.

He made it a daily thing, not a one-time heroic gesture: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me” (Luke 9:23). The cost of following Jesus is not usually martyrdom; it is the daily death of self-will — the surrender of the right to run your own life, choose your own way, and keep back anything he asks for.

What it actually costs

For some the cost has been dramatic. Missionaries like David Brainerd spent themselves to exhaustion; his Life and Diary records a young man pouring out his health and his years for the salvation of others, dying at twenty-nine, having counted his own comfort as nothing beside Christ. Amy Carmichael, in Things as They Are, refused to soften the hard realities of the mission field for comfortable supporters back home, and gave her whole life without a furlough home. Hudson Taylor left everything familiar for inland China and buried a wife and children in that soil.

But for most of us the cost is quieter and no less real: the ambition laid down, the relationship surrendered to God, the sin we loved given up, the reputation risked, the money held loosely, the plans reshaped by his call. Jesus was clear that it reaches even our dearest loves — not that we hate family, but that no one, not even those closest to us, can hold the place that belongs to him alone. To follow him is to hand over the title deed to your life.

Why he was so honest about it

Why did Jesus scare off the half-hearted? Because a disciple who has not counted the cost will abandon him at the first hard turn, and because he was offering something too valuable to be received casually. He told two tiny parables about it: a man finds treasure hidden in a field and “in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44). Note the emotion — joy. The man does not grieve over selling everything; he can hardly believe his luck. That is how Jesus wants the cost understood: not as a grim price grudgingly paid, but as everything-you-have traded for something worth infinitely more.

This is the paradox at the heart of it: “whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25). The self we cling to, we lose; the self we surrender to Christ, we finally receive back, alive. The cost is real, but it is the cost of exchanging fool’s gold for the genuine article.

Why it is worth everything

The witnesses are unanimous. Paul, who lost career, status, comfort, and finally his life, wrote from prison: “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). Not I gritted my teeth and paid, but I count it loss — the way you’d count last year’s trash beside this year’s inheritance. Jesus himself promised that nothing given up for him goes unrepaid: “there is no one who has left house or brothers … for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time … and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10:29–30). A hundredfold, now and forever — that is the exchange rate Jesus offers, and no one who has taken him up on it has ever complained of a bad deal.

The reason the cost is worth it, finally, is not the size of the reward but the worth of the One received. To follow Jesus is not mainly to give things up in order to get better things; it is to get Christ himself — and everything else, kept or surrendered, is thrown into shadow beside that. This is why the sufferings of Brainerd, Carmichael, and Taylor read not as tragedies but as trades gladly made. They were not miserable people who had lost everything; they were the freest, most joyful people of their generation, because they had found the pearl of great price and let all the cheaper beads fall from their hands. The world looks at the cost and sees only loss. Those who have paid it look back and see only gain — and wonder that God let them in on such a bargain at all.

Hudson Taylor, looking back over a life that cost him nearly everything, called it in A Retrospect not a sacrifice but a privilege; he insisted he had never made a sacrifice at all, so richly had God repaid every surrender. That is the testimony of those who actually paid the price — not regret, but wonder that they were let in on such a bargain.

The cost of not following

We are quick to tally what discipleship costs and slow to reckon the other side of the ledger: the cost of not following. Jesus put the two side by side. The man who keeps his life, refusing the cross, does not thereby save it — “whoever would save his life will lose it” (Matthew 16:25). There is no cost-free option. To decline Jesus’ terms is not to avoid loss; it is to choose a different and far greater loss — to spend your one life on things that cannot keep it, and to arrive at the end having gained the world, if you were fortunate, and forfeited your soul.

Seen that way, counting the cost cuts both directions. Yes, following Jesus will cost you your self-rule, your sin, and sometimes your comfort and reputation. But not following costs you Christ, and everything he is and gives — forgiveness, a Father, a purpose that outlives you, and a life that death cannot end. When the treasure in the field is real, the truly expensive thing is to walk away and keep your pocket change. The person who “in his joy” sold everything (Matthew 13:44) was not the one who paid too much; the fool in the story is the one who saw the treasure and kept his coins. The cost of discipleship is high. The cost of refusing it is higher.

The honest invitation

So the invitation of Jesus is not the soft thing we sometimes make it. It asks for everything: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). But it gives back more than it asks — a life no longer spent on itself, a treasure that cannot be lost, and Christ himself, in whom “the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). Count the cost, by all means; Jesus told you to. Then count what you gain. And you will understand why, across twenty centuries, those who gave him everything have said, with one voice, that they would not trade places with a king.
